CH2 · UNIT 03 · MODULE 3.3

Mendelian Genetics

How Mendel's pea crosses revealed the two rules of inheritance, how both rules come straight from meiosis, and how to predict any cross with probability and Punnett squares. Part 1 is Mendel's experiments. Part 2 is one gene: segregation. Part 3 is two or more genes: independent assortment.

BEFORE YOU START This module builds on Module 3.2, Meiosis & Mutations: alleles, homologous chromosomes, and how they separate in meiosis I.

MODULE 3.3 · PART 1

Mendel's experiments

THE QUESTION Breeders had crossed plants for centuries without finding rules. What did Mendel do differently, and what did he see?

In this part: the big picture of the whole module, Mendel's three choices and his seven traits, then the parental, F1 and F2 generations.

THE BIG PICTURE

How it all fits: what Mendel saw, why it happens, how to predict

There's a lot to keep track of in this module. It all hangs on one idea from the textbook: the laws of inheritance are what chromosomes do in meiosis. Mendel saw ratios; meiosis explains them; the tools predict them.1,2

1 · WHAT MENDEL SAWRatios in the offspringOne trait: F1 all one kind, F2 3 : 1. Two traits: F2 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
2 · WHY: CHROMOSOMES IN MEIOSISTwo laws, two moments in meiosis ISegregation: homologs separate in anaphase I, so each gamete gets one allele. Independent assortment: each pair lines up at random in metaphase I, so the alleles of different genes mix.
3 · HOW TO PREDICTThe toolsGametes → Punnett square or AND / OR rules → ratios. Testcross to reveal a genotype. 2ⁿ to count gamete kinds.

Which tool for which question?

THE QUESTIONTHE TOOL
What gametes can it make?Segregation: one allele of each gene per gamete. Independent assortment: every combination. Count kinds with 2ⁿ (n = heterozygous genes). Go
What offspring, in what ratio?A Punnett square, or the AND rule (multiply) and OR rule (add). Go
Two genes at once?Solve each gene on its own, then multiply (two small squares). Go
What is its hidden genotype?A testcross: cross it with a homozygous recessive. Go
Which law does this cell show?Homologs separating = segregation. Pairs lined up different ways = independent assortment. Go
START HERE

Why Mendel saw what others missed

Gregor Mendel, a monk in Brno, crossed garden peas (Pisum sativum) from 1856 to 1863. Plant breeders had done hybridization experiments before him, but none found rules. Mendel did, because of three choices.3,4

INTERACTIVE · THREE CHOICES

How Mendel set up his experiments

Tap a button to explore
1 · TRUE-BREEDING STRAINSStart from strains that never changeEach strain Mendel used was true-breeding: bred among themselves, yellow-seeded plants gave only yellow seeds, generation after generation. Others used complex, poorly defined plants.
2 · ONE TRAIT AT A TIMEFollow one contrasting traitHe followed one trait (or a few) with easily contrasted forms, such as yellow vs. green seeds. Breeders who followed many traits at once saw inheritance so complicated that no pattern showed.
3 · COUNT THE OFFSPRINGLook for numbersHe counted every offspring and looked for statistical patterns. Others only noted whether a trait was present or absent. Counting is what revealed 3 : 1 and 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
TAP ONEThree things he did differentlyTap each to see what it gave him.
THE SEVEN TRAITS

Seven pairs of contrasting traits

IGNORED, THEN REDISCOVEREDMendel's work was ignored during his lifetime. Its importance was recognized only in 1900, 16 years after his death, and that rediscovery marks the start of modern genetics.
CROSSING PEASPea flowers usually fertilize themselves. To cross two plants, Mendel opened a flower early and cut off its immature anthers (the male parts), dusted its stigma with pollen from the chosen father plant, and tied a cloth bag over it to keep stray pollen out. Each fertilized ovule became one pea in the pod.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Hybridization

Interbreeding between two different varieties (strains) or species. Mendel's crosses between true-breeding strains are hybridizations, and their offspring are hybrids.

True-breeding

A strain whose offspring look the same as the parents, generation after generation, when bred among themselves: homozygous for the trait.

THE FIRST CROSSES

P, F1, F2: one trait disappears and comes back

Mendel crossed true-breeding strains that differed in one trait. The result in the first generation was always the same: only one of the two traits showed.3,1

INTERACTIVE · 3 GENERATIONS

Seed color, generation by generation

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
PARENTAL CROSSTrue-breeding yellow × true-breeding greenThe parental (P) generation: yellow AA × green aa. Mendel made the cross both ways (yellow pollen on green flowers and the reverse, a reciprocal cross) and got the same result.
F1 GENERATIONAll yellowEvery F1 seed was yellow, so yellow is dominant and green is recessive. The F1 are hybrids: each got A from the yellow parent and a from the green, so all are Aa.
F2 GENERATIONGreen comes back, 3 : 1Mendel let the F1 self-fertilize (the F1 cross). In the F2, green reappeared: 6,022 yellow to 2,001 green, 3.01 : 1. All seven traits gave close to 3 : 1.
Check yourself: Why do we often say recessive traits "skip a generation"?

In the parental and F1 crosses, the recessive trait (green) disappears in the F1, because every F1 is Aa and one A is enough to make the seed yellow. The F1 still carry a, so when they are crossed, a quarter of the F2 are aa and green: the trait "skipped" the F1 and reappeared in the F2.

Check yourself: When two true-breeding parents are crossed, how can you tell which trait is dominant?

Look at the F1. The trait that shows in all the F1 is dominant; the one that disappears is recessive. With two genes, do it for each trait separately: yellow × green gave yellow F1, so yellow is dominant; wrinkled × round gave round F1, so round is dominant.

WHY YELLOW IS DOMINANTYellow peas make an enzyme that breaks down green chlorophyll. The green allele is a mutation that inactivates the enzyme. In an Aa seed, one working copy makes enough enzyme to clear the chlorophyll, so the seed is yellow.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Parental (P) generation

The first generation in a series of crosses: here the true-breeding parents (written P or P₁).

Parental cross

The cross between the two parents of the P generation, for example true-breeding yellow AA × true-breeding green aa. It produces the F1.

F1 generation

The first filial generation: the offspring of the parental cross. When the parents are true-breeding for different traits, all F1 are heterozygous hybrids and show the dominant trait.

F1 cross

A cross between F1 individuals (or an F1 self-fertilized), for example Aa × Aa. It produces the F2.

F2 generation

The second filial generation: the offspring of the F1 cross. The recessive trait reappears in the F2.

F2 cross

A cross between F2 individuals (or an F2 self-fertilized). Mendel self-fertilized F2 plants to tell the true-breeding AA from the Aa.

Dominant

The trait (or allele) that shows in the F1 when two true-breeding strains are crossed; one copy of the dominant allele is enough to give the trait. Written with a capital letter (A).

Recessive

The trait (or allele) that does not show in the F1, and shows only in homozygotes (aa). Written with a lowercase letter (a).

Lock it in · Part 1

  1. Mendel succeeded because he used true-breeding strains, followed one trait at a time, and counted the offspring.
  2. Parental cross (true-breeding AA × aa) → F1, all Aa, all showing the dominant trait.
  3. F1 cross (Aa × Aa) → F2, with the recessive trait back in a 3 : 1 ratio: it "skips a generation".
  4. The trait that shows in the F1 of two true-breeding parents is the dominant one.

MODULE 3.3 · PART 2

One gene: the principle of segregation

THE QUESTION Why does a trait that vanishes in the F1 come back in exactly a quarter of the F2?

In this part: one chromosome pair followed from P to F2, the law of segregation and where it happens in meiosis, why one parent's 1/2 becomes 1/4 in the offspring, predicting crosses with probability, and the Punnett square.

FOLLOW THE CHROMOSOMES

Segregation, tracked: one chromosome pair from P to F2

The textbook puts it in one line: "Segregation of alleles reflects the separation of chromosomes in meiosis." Watch one pair of chromosomes travel through two generations. Gold chromosomes came from the yellow-seed parent, green ones from the green-seed parent.1

INTERACTIVE · 6 STAGES · ONE GENE

From true-breeding parents to 3 : 1

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 6
P GENERATIONTwo true-breeding parentsA true-breeding yellow plant is AA: both chromosomes of the pair carry A. A true-breeding green plant is aa. Both are diploid: two of each chromosome.
MEIOSIS IN THE PARENTSOne chromosome per gameteMeiosis puts one chromosome of each pair into each gamete. An AA plant has only A to give, so every gamete is A; every aa gamete is a.
FERTILIZATION · F1One from each parentAn A gamete meets an a gamete: every F1 plant is Aa, with one gold and one green chromosome. All are yellow because A is dominant, but the a allele is still there, hidden.
ANAPHASE I IN THE F1This is segregationIn an F1 germ cell, the homologs separate in anaphase I: the A chromosome goes one way, the a chromosome the other. That physical separation is Mendel's law of segregation.
THE F1'S GAMETESHalf A, half aAfter meiosis II, half the F1's gametes carry A and half carry a. That 1 : 1 is the whole secret of the 3 : 1.
F2Random union gives 1 : 2 : 1Any egg can meet any sperm: AA, Aa, aA, aa, equally likely. Genotypes 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa; phenotypes 3 yellow : 1 green. The green trait "skipped" the F1 and came back, because the F1 carried it hidden.
THE ONE IDEAEvery Mendel problem is this movie: parents → gametes (one allele each) → fertilization (one from each parent) → offspring. The probability rules and the Punnett square just work through the last two steps.
MENDEL'S FIRST LAW

The principle of segregation

Mendel explained 3 : 1 with a few simple ideas, written here in today's words. The last one is the Law of Segregation, and meiosis is the reason it works.1,2

1Two alleles per geneEach body cell has two alleles of every gene, at the same locus on two homologs. True-breeding plants are homozygous (AA or aa); the F1 are heterozygous (Aa).
2One allele per gameteEach gamete carries only one allele of each gene: A or a, never both.
3They segregate equallyThe two alleles segregate equally into gametes: an Aa plant makes 1/2 A gametes and 1/2 a gametes.
4Random unionA zygote forms from the random union of one gamete from each parent.
INTERACTIVE · MEIOSIS IN AN F1 PLANT

Where segregation happens

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
THE GERM CELLOne A, one aAn F1 plant's germ cell has the A allele on one homolog and the a allele on the other.
AFTER S PHASEBoth alleles copiedEach chromosome is now two sister chromatids: A A on one homolog, a a on the other.
ANAPHASE ISegregation, physicallyThe homologous chromosomes separate in anaphase I, so the A copies go to one pole and the a copies to the other. This separation is the segregation Mendel inferred from his ratios.
THE GAMETESHalf A, half aAfter meiosis II, two gametes carry A and two carry a: 1/2 A, 1/2 a, exactly as the law predicts.
Check yourself: Where in meiosis does segregation occur? How does the law of segregation help us predict the alleles in gametes?

In anaphase I, when homologous chromosomes separate. Because the two alleles always go to different gametes in equal numbers, we can predict gametes from a genotype: AA → all A; aa → all a; Aa → 1/2 A and 1/2 a.

LOOK BACK
MODULE 3.2 · MEIOSIS & MUTATIONSMeiosis, stage by stage →Anaphase I is where homologs separate.MODULE 3.2 · MEIOSIS & MUTATIONSHomologs, chromatids and ploidy →Alleles sit at the same locus on homologous chromosomes.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Allele

One version of a gene: a variation of the gene's DNA sequence at a particular place on a chromosome. Mendel's "hereditary factors".

Locus

The place on a chromosome where a gene sits. The two alleles of a gene in a diploid cell are at the same locus on the two homologs.

Genotype

The combination of alleles an individual has for a gene (or genes): AA, Aa or aa.

Phenotype

The observable trait: yellow or green seeds. AA and Aa can have the same phenotype.

Homozygous

Having two identical alleles of a gene: AA or aa.

Heterozygous

Having two different alleles of a gene: Aa.

Gamete

A haploid reproductive cell (egg, sperm, or the ovule's egg and the pollen's sperm in plants) carrying one allele of each gene.

Zygote

The fertilized egg, formed by the random union of two gametes, one from each parent. It has two alleles of each gene.

Segregate

To separate. The two alleles of a gene segregate into different gametes, because homologous chromosomes separate in anaphase I.

Mendel's Law of Segregation

The two alleles of a gene separate (segregate) equally into gametes, so half the gametes carry one allele and half carry the other.

ONE PARENT, THEN TWO

From 1/2 to 1/4: why two A gametes don't mean AA is 1/2

The dividing cell shows 2 A and 2 a, which is 1/2. Yet AA is 1/4. Both are right, because they answer different questions: one is about a gamete from one parent, the other about an offspring from two parents.1,2

WALK THROUGH IT · 5 STEPS · THREE GENERATIONS

From one cell's gametes to one offspring

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 5
LOOK BACK A GENERATIONThe A and a came from this plant's own parentsThe cell in the slides is already Aa because of an earlier fertilization: one AA parent, one aa parent. That mother and father are finished. They are not the two sets in the calculation.
ONE PARENT · ONE MEIOSISp(A gamete) = 1/2This one plant's cell copies its DNA, then divides twice, ending in A, A, a, a. 2 of 4 gametes carry A. That 1/2 is about one gamete.
THE SECOND SETNow two Aa plants mateA new plant takes one gamete from its mother and one from its father. So there are two separate meioses, one in each F1 parent, each giving 1/2 A and 1/2 a. This is the other set you need to consider.
BOTH MUST HAPPENp(AA) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4AA needs an A egg and an A sperm. Getting an A from one parent doesn't guarantee an A from the other, so you multiply.
SEE IT AS FRACTIONSHalf of a halfHalf of all offspring got an A egg. Only half of those also got an A sperm. That leaves a quarter of all the offspring: AA.
COMMON MIX-UP"2 of 4 gametes are A, so isn't AA 1/2?" No. 1/2 is the share of one parent's gametes. AA is an offspring, which takes one gamete from each of two parents, so you multiply: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
Check yourself: An Aa plant: what fraction of its gametes carry a? Two Aa plants mate: what fraction of offspring are aa?

1/2 of one plant's gametes carry a. 1/4 of the offspring are aa: an a egg (1/2) AND an a sperm (1/2).

PREDICT IT

Predicting crosses with probability: genotype and phenotype ratios

The law of segregation says what the gametes are, and that is all you need to predict a cross. Every probability is between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain), and two rules combine them.1,2

INTERACTIVE · Aa × Aa

From gametes to ratios

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 5
THE GAMETESHalf A, half aAn Aa parent gives A 1/2 and a 1/2, because the alleles segregate.
BOTH/AND = MULTIPLYOne egg AND one spermEach offspring needs an egg and a sperm. They are independent events, so multiply: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
EITHER/OR = ADDTwo ways to be AaA from mom and a from dad, or a from mom and A from dad. They can't both happen, so add: 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2.
GENOTYPE RATIO1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aaA genotype ratio counts allele combinations: 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa, 1/4 aa.
PHENOTYPE RATIO3 dominant : 1 recessiveA phenotype ratio counts what you see. A is dominant, so AA and Aa are both yellow: 1/4 + 1/2 = 3/4. Only aa shows the recessive green: 1/4.
Check yourself: How do the 'both/and' and 'either/or' rules work?

Both/and: for independent events that happen together, multiply (A from mom AND a from dad: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4). Either/or: for outcomes that can't happen at the same time, add (AA or Aa: 1/4 + 1/2 = 3/4).

Check yourself: What is the difference between a genotype ratio and a phenotype ratio?

A genotype ratio counts allele combinations (1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa). A phenotype ratio counts how the offspring look (3 yellow : 1 green). With dominance, different genotypes can share a phenotype, so the ratios differ.

Check yourself: Xeroderma pigmentosum is a recessive skin condition. A woman homozygous for the dominant allele and a homozygous man with the condition have a child. Chance the child has it?

0%. Call the alleles P (dominant) and p (the condition). The woman is PP and gives only P; the man is pp and gives only p. Every child is Pp: a carrier who doesn't have the condition.

INTERACTIVE · THE TEXTBOOK'S POD OF FOUR PEAS

The same two rules, used together

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
EITHER/OR = ADDOutcomes that can't happen togetherOne seed can't be both AA and Aa, so the chance it is AA or Aa is 1/4 + 1/2 = 3/4.
BOTH/AND = MULTIPLYIndependent events togetherEach seed comes from a separate fertilization, so they are independent. The chance the seed by the stem is green and the other three yellow: 1/4 × 3/4 × 3/4 × 3/4 = 27/256.
USE BOTHExactly one green, any positionThe green seed can be in any of 4 positions (OR), each with probability 27/256 (AND): 4 × 27/256 = 108/256, about 42%.
Check yourself: True-breeding yellow × true-breeding green gives all-yellow F1. If the F1 self-cross, what fraction of the F2 is yellow AND heterozygous?

1/2. Every Aa seed is yellow, and p(Aa) = 1/2.

KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Carrier

A heterozygous individual (Aa) who carries one copy of a recessive allele without showing the recessive trait, and can pass it on.

Dominant

The trait (or allele) that shows in the F1 when two true-breeding strains are crossed; one copy of the dominant allele is enough to give the trait. Written with a capital letter (A).

Recessive

The trait (or allele) that does not show in the F1, and shows only in homozygotes (aa). Written with a lowercase letter (a).

SAME ANSWER, AS A PICTURE

The Punnett square: those probabilities in a grid

A Punnett square is a picture of the probabilities you just worked out: the same four outcomes, laid out as a grid. For the F1 cross Aa × Aa, a monohybrid cross (both parents heterozygous for the one gene traced), it gives Mendel's 3 : 1.1,2

INTERACTIVE · Aa × Aa

Build the square

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 5
THE OUTSIDEThe gametesLetters on the outside are one parent's gametes across the top and the other parent's down the side, each with its probability: an Aa parent gives A 1/2 and a 1/2.
THE INSIDEThe offspringEach box inside is a zygote: the gamete in its row joined with the gamete in its column. Its probability is the row's × the column's: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
GENOTYPE RATIO1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aaCount the genotypes: 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa, 1/4 aa. Aa appears twice (A from the egg and a from the sperm, or the reverse).
PHENOTYPE: YELLOW3/4AA and Aa both look yellow, so 3 boxes of 4 are yellow. Among the yellow ones, 1/3 are AA and 2/3 are Aa.
PHENOTYPE: GREEN1/4Only aa is green: 1 box of 4. So the phenotype ratio is 3 yellow : 1 green.
Check yourself: What do the letters on the outside and the inside of a Punnett square represent?

Outside: the alleles in each parent's gametes (one parent across the top, the other down the side), with their frequencies. Inside: the genotypes of the offspring, each made by one gamete from each parent.

HE TESTED ITThe square predicts that among yellow F2 seeds, 1/3 are AA (true-breeding) and 2/3 are Aa. Mendel self-fertilized yellow F2 plants (an F2 cross): 166 bred true and 353 gave some green, close to 1 : 2.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Punnett square

A grid for predicting a cross: one parent's gametes and their frequencies go across the top, the other's down the side, and each box is a possible offspring genotype. Named after the British geneticist Reginald Punnett.

Monohybrid cross

A cross in which both parents are heterozygous for the one gene being traced: Aa × Aa. (This course's definition.)

Lock it in · Part 2

  1. Segregation: the two alleles of a gene separate equally into gametes (1/2 A, 1/2 a). It happens in anaphase I, when homologs separate.
  2. 1/2 is about one gamete from one parent. 1/4 is about one offspring from two parents: an A egg (1/2) AND an A sperm (1/2).
  3. Gametes first: Aa gives 1/2 A, 1/2 a. Both/and → multiply (independent events). Either/or → add (outcomes that can't happen together).
  4. Aa × Aa (a monohybrid cross): genotypes 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa; phenotypes 3 dominant : 1 recessive.
  5. A Punnett square is the same probabilities as a grid: gametes outside, offspring inside.

MODULE 3.3 · PART 3

Two or more genes: independent assortment

THE QUESTION When two traits are followed at once, does inheriting one affect inheriting the other?

In this part: the 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 cross, two chromosome pairs followed from P to F2, independent assortment in meiosis, then one question solved three ways (probability, one big square, two small squares), the testcross, working backwards, and three or more genes.

TWO TRAITS

Two genes at once: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1

Next Mendel crossed strains differing in two traits: seed color (A yellow, a green) and seed shape (B round, b wrinkled).1,2

INTERACTIVE · 3 GENERATIONS

Yellow wrinkled × green round

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
PARENTAL CROSSAA bb × aa BBTrue-breeding yellow wrinkled (AA bb) × true-breeding green round (aa BB). Each parent makes only one kind of gamete: Ab and aB.
F1All yellow and round: Aa BbEvery F1 seed is yellow (A dominant) and round (B dominant), heterozygous for both genes. Crossing two of them, Aa Bb × Aa Bb, is a dihybrid cross.
F2Four phenotypes, 9 : 3 : 3 : 1Of 639 F2 seeds: 367 yellow round, 122 green round, 113 yellow wrinkled, 37 green wrinkled, about 9.9 : 3.3 : 3.1 : 1. Two combinations (yellow wrinkled, green round) were in the parents; two (yellow round, green wrinkled) are new.
Check yourself: What cross gives you a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 phenotypic ratio?

A dihybrid cross: AaBb × AaBb, both parents heterozygous for two genes that assort independently, each with a dominant and a recessive allele, affecting different traits.

WHY 9 : 3 : 3 : 1Treat each gene separately: color is 3/4 yellow : 1/4 green, shape is 3/4 round : 1/4 wrinkled. Combine with the AND rule: yellow round 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16; yellow wrinkled 3/4 × 1/4 = 3/16; green round 1/4 × 3/4 = 3/16; green wrinkled 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16.
COMMON MIX-UPKeep genotype and phenotype apart when tracing two genes. "Yellow round" is a phenotype that four genotypes give (AABB, AABb, AaBB, AaBb). Write it as A_ B_, where _ means either allele.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Dihybrid cross

A cross tracing two genes in which both parents are heterozygous for both: AaBb × AaBb. (This course's definition.) It gives a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 phenotype ratio.

FOLLOW THE CHROMOSOMES

Independent assortment, tracked: two chromosome pairs from P to F2

The textbook again: "Independent assortment reflects the random alignment of chromosomes in meiosis." Same movie as before, with two genes on two different chromosome pairs: seed color (A) on a long pair, seed shape (B) on a short pair.1

INTERACTIVE · 6 STAGES · TWO GENES

From AABB × aabb to 9 : 3 : 3 : 1

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 6
P GENERATIONTwo genes, two pairsA true-breeding yellow round plant (AABB) crossed with a true-breeding green wrinkled plant (aabb). Gene A is on one chromosome pair, gene B on another.
MEIOSIS IN THE PARENTSOne of each pairEach gamete gets one chromosome of each pair. The gold parent can only give AB; the green parent only ab.
F1AaBb, all yellow roundEvery F1 plant is AaBb: a gold and a green chromosome of each pair. Both dominant traits show.
METAPHASE I IN THE F1Two ways to line upIn each F1 germ cell the two pairs line up at the middle. The gold chromosomes can face the same pole (gametes AB and ab) or opposite poles (gametes Ab and aB). Which way each pair faces is random and doesn't depend on the other pair: independent assortment.
THE F1'S GAMETESFour kinds, 1/4 eachOne germ cell makes only 2 kinds, but across all the F1's germ cells both ways happen equally: AB, Ab, aB, ab, 1/4 each. Ab and aB are new combinations that neither P parent had.
F29 : 3 : 3 : 1Four kinds of eggs × four kinds of sperm = 16 equally likely combinations, sorting into 9 yellow round : 3 yellow wrinkled : 3 green round : 1 green wrinkled. The next sections show how to get there with squares and the AND rule.
MENDEL'S SECOND LAW

Independent assortment comes from meiosis

The Law of Independent Assortment: the alleles of one gene segregate into gametes independently of the alleles of another. For genes on different chromosomes, the reason is metaphase I: each homologous pair lines up independently of the others.1,3

INTERACTIVE · AN AaBb GERM CELL, 2n = 4

Two ways to line up

Tap a button to explore
WAY 1 · HALF OF ALL GERM CELLSAB and abA and B face the same pole: this cell's gametes are AB and ab.
WAY 2 · THE OTHER HALFAb and aBThe short pair is flipped: this cell's gametes are Ab and aB.
ACROSS MANY GERM CELLS1/4 eachBoth ways are equally likely, so over many cells: AB, Ab, aB, ab, 1/4 each. With the AND rule: p(AB) = p(A) × p(B) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
TAP ONEWhich way will the pairs face?Pink came from the mother, blue from the father. Each pair's orientation is random.
Check yourself: Where in meiosis does independent assortment occur? How does it help predict the alleles in gametes?

In metaphase I (with the separation in anaphase I): each homologous pair lines up independently, so which allele of gene A goes to a pole doesn't affect which allele of gene B goes with it. So an AaBb individual makes AB, Ab, aB and ab gametes in equal proportions, 1/4 each.

Check yourself: 2n = 4, heterozygous for two genes on separate chromosomes. How many kinds of gametes can one germ cell make? The whole organism?

One germ cell: 2 kinds (it lines up one way only: AB + ab, or Ab + aB). The whole organism: 4 kinds (AB, Ab, aB, ab), because different germ cells line up different ways.

Check yourself: Do chromosomes assort independently during mitosis?

No. Homologs never pair in mitosis; sister chromatids separate, and both daughter cells get every chromosome. Independent assortment happens only in meiosis I.

ONE CELL, PAIRS SEPARATINGSegregationA cell in anaphase I with A pulled from a and B from b shows the law of segregation. (One cell shows only one orientation.)
TWO CELLS, DIFFERENT WAYSBoth lawsTwo cells lined up different ways, each separating its homologs, show both segregation and independent assortment.
NONDISJUNCTION IN MEIOSIS IBreaks segregationIf the A/a pair fails to separate in meiosis I, A and a go to the same gamete: the law of segregation is violated.
Check yourself: Why is nondisjunction during meiosis II not a violation of independent assortment?

Independent assortment happens in meiosis I, when the homologous pairs line up and separate. By meiosis II the combination of maternal and paternal chromosomes in each cell has already been chosen at random. Nondisjunction in meiosis II only fails to separate sister chromatids, copies of the same allele, so it changes how many copies a gamete gets, not which combination of different genes' alleles travel together.

NOT EVERY GENEGenes close together on the same chromosome usually travel together and do not assort independently: they are linked. That comes in a later module.
LOOK BACK
MODULE 3.2 · MEIOSIS & MUTATIONSIndependent assortment in meiosis →The same picture, with 2ⁿ combinations.MODULE 3.2 · MEIOSIS & MUTATIONSNondisjunction →What goes wrong in meiosis I and II.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment

The segregation of one gene's alleles is independent of the segregation of another gene's alleles (for genes on different chromosomes), so all combinations of alleles appear in gametes in equal proportions.

PREDICT IT

Two genes with probability: both/and, gene by gene

Because the genes assort independently, a two-gene problem is just two one-gene problems. Take one question: brown long-tailed BbLl mice mate. What fraction of the offspring are also BbLl?1,3

INTERACTIVE · MICE: BbLl × BbLl

One gene, then the other, then multiply

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
FURp(Bb) = 1/2Two ways to be Bb, 1/4 each. Either/or, so add.
TAILp(Ll) = 1/2The same math, because the tail gene assorts independently of the fur gene.
BOTHp(BbLl) = 1/4Bb and Ll, so multiply: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
Check yourself: True-breeding brown long-tailed mice × true-breeding yellow short-tailed mice give all brown long-tailed F1. If two F1 mate, what fraction of their offspring have the F1 genotype?

The F1 are BbLl. p(Bb) = 1/2 and p(Ll) = 1/2. p(BbLl) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 = 4/16.

SAME ANSWER, AS A PICTURE

One big Punnett square: 16 boxes

You can also draw every combination. Each heterozygous parent makes four kinds of gametes, 1/4 each, so the square needs 4 rows and 4 columns: 16 equally likely boxes. It gives the same answer: AaBb is 4 of the 16 boxes, or 1/4.1

INTERACTIVE · AaBb × AaBb

Find each class

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 6
THE WHOLE SQUARE16 boxes, 9 genotypes, 4 phenotypesEach box is 1/16. The 9 genotypes come in the ratio 1 AABB : 2 AABb : 1 AAbb : 2 AaBB : 4 AaBb : 2 Aabb : 1 aaBB : 2 aaBb : 1 aabb.
YELLOW, ROUND9/16Every box with at least one A and at least one B (A_ B_).
YELLOW, WRINKLED3/16At least one A, and bb (A_ bb).
GREEN, ROUND3/16aa, and at least one B (aa B_).
GREEN, WRINKLED1/16Only aa bb.
SAME AS THE F1AaBb: 4/164 of the 16 boxes are Aa Bb, the F1's genotype.
Check yourself: How many rows and columns do you need in a Punnett square?

One row for each kind of gamete one parent can make, and one column for each kind the other parent can make. Aa × Aa: 2 × 2. AaBb × AaBb: 4 × 4. AaBb × aabb: 4 × 1.

DATA, NOT JUST THEORYMendel tested this too: he self-fertilized F2 plants and classified each as true-breeding or segregating for each trait. The numbers fit the 1 : 2 : 1 : 2 : 4 : 2 : 1 : 2 : 1 genotype ratio within the margins expected by chance.
THE SHORTCUT

Two small squares and the AND rule

The third way to the same answer: one 2 × 2 square for each gene, then multiply. Two small squares replace one 4 × 4.1,3

INTERACTIVE · MICE: BbLl × BbLl

Brown long × brown long

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
FURBb × BbB (brown) is dominant to b (yellow). Bb is 2 of the 4 boxes: p(Bb) = 1/2.
TAILLl × LlL (long) is dominant to l (short). Ll is 2 of the 4 boxes: p(Ll) = 1/2.
COMBINE WITH AND1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4An offspring that is Bb and Ll: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 = 4/16, the same as counting 4 boxes in the big square.
Check yourself: When might you use two Punnett squares together instead of one big one?

Whenever the genes assort independently (different chromosomes). It is faster and less error-prone, especially when you want one particular genotype or phenotype, or when there are three or more genes (a big square would have 64 or more boxes).

WHAT'S HIDDEN?

The testcross

A yellow seed could be AA or Aa: same phenotype, different genotype. A testcross tells them apart by crossing the unknown with a homozygous recessive, which can only give a.4

INTERACTIVE · UNKNOWN YELLOW × aa

Two possible answers

Tap a button to explore
IF THE UNKNOWN IS AAAll yellowAn AA parent gives only A gametes, so every offspring is Aa and yellow.
IF THE UNKNOWN IS AaHalf yellow, half greenAn Aa parent gives A and a equally, so half the offspring are Aa (yellow) and half aa (green). Mendel's testcrosses of heterozygotes gave 196 yellow : 189 green, close to 1 : 1.
TAP ONEWhat will the offspring look like?The recessive parent adds only a, so the offspring show exactly which alleles the unknown parent gave.
Check yourself: What is a testcross and what does it allow you to figure out?

A cross of an individual with an unknown genotype to a homozygous recessive individual. It reveals the unknown's genotype: all dominant offspring → homozygous dominant (AA); about half recessive → heterozygous (Aa). It also directly shows segregation (a 1 : 1 ratio).

COMMON MIX-UPCross the unknown with the homozygous recessive, not the dominant. AA × AA and Aa × AA both give all-dominant offspring, so a dominant tester can't tell them apart.
KEY TERMS · TAP ONE TO OPEN IT
Testcross

A cross of an individual with an unknown genotype to a homozygous recessive individual. The offspring's phenotypes reveal the unknown parent's gametes, and so its genotype.

WORK BACKWARDS

Testcrosses with two genes

The offspring of a cross tell you about the parents. A testcross with an aabb (here bbll) tester shows exactly which gametes the unknown parent made, one gene at a time.1,3

INTERACTIVE · A CAPTURED MOUSE

What is its genotype?

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
THE CROSSUnknown × bbllA captured brown, long-tailed mouse (B_ L_) is crossed with a mouse true-breeding for yellow fur and a short tail (bbll), which only gives bl gametes.
THE OFFSPRINGAll brown; half long, half shortAll offspring have brown fur. Half have long tails, half short.
THE ANSWERBB LlFur: no yellow offspring, so the mouse never gave b: BB. Tail: half short, so it gave l half the time: Ll.
Check yourself: You capture a brown, long-tailed mouse. What single cross tells you its genotype?

Unknown × homozygous recessive (bbll): a testcross. A homozygous dominant tester would give all brown, long-tailed offspring whatever the unknown is.

Check yourself: For TtRr × ttrr, which genotype would you NOT expect: ttrr, TtRr, Ttrr, ttRr or TtRR?

TtRR. The ttrr parent gives only tr, so no offspring can have two R alleles. The four expected genotypes are TtRr, Ttrr, ttRr and ttrr, 1/4 each (TtRr makes 4 gamete types; ttrr makes 1).

THREE OR MORE GENES

Counting gametes and offspring for many genes

Independent assortment works for any number of genes on different chromosomes. Two counting tricks handle them.1,3

INTERACTIVE · BRANCHING

How many kinds of gamete?

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 2
3 HETEROZYGOUS GENES2³ = 8Each heterozygous gene doubles the number of gamete types: BLR, BLr, BlR, Blr, bLR, bLr, blR, blr.
2 HETEROZYGOUS GENES2² = 4A homozygous gene (BB) gives only one allele, so it doesn't branch. n counts only the heterozygous genes: BLR, BLr, BlR, Blr.
Check yourself: How can you figure out the number of unique gamete genotypes for an organism heterozygous for 3 or more genes? What about a mix of heterozygous and homozygous genes?

Use 2ⁿ, where n is the number of heterozygous genes (each gamete gets one allele of each gene, and each heterozygous gene gives 2 choices). BbLlRr: 2³ = 8. BBLlRr: homozygous genes add no variety, so n = 2 and 2² = 4.

Check yourself: AaBBCcDd × AaBbCcdd (all on different chromosomes). Expected frequency of aaBBccdd?

One gene at a time, then multiply: aa from Aa × Aa = 1/4; BB from BB × Bb = 1/2; cc from Cc × Cc = 1/4; dd from Dd × dd = 1/2. 1/4 × 1/2 × 1/4 × 1/2 = 1/64.

Lock it in · Part 3

  1. Dihybrid cross (AaBb × AaBb) → phenotypes 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 (9 A_B_ : 3 A_bb : 3 aaB_ : 1 aabb); 9 genotypes.
  2. Independent assortment: each gene's alleles segregate independently of another's (genes on different chromosomes), because homologous pairs line up independently in metaphase I. AaBb → AB, Ab, aB, ab, 1/4 each.
  3. One germ cell makes 2 kinds of gamete; the whole organism makes all 4.
  4. Three ways to the same answer: probability gene by gene, one big square (rows × columns = gamete types of each parent), or two small squares combined with AND.
  5. A testcross (unknown × homozygous recessive) reveals the unknown genotype: all dominant → homozygous; half recessive → heterozygous. With two genes, read one gene at a time.
  6. Gamete types = 2ⁿ, n = number of heterozygous genes.

Vocab · 26 terms
Allele One version of a gene: a variation of the gene's DNA sequence at a particular place on a chromosome. Mendel's "hereditary factors".
Carrier A heterozygous individual (Aa) who carries one copy of a recessive allele without showing the recessive trait, and can pass it on.
Dominant The trait (or allele) that shows in the F1 when two true-breeding strains are crossed; one copy of the dominant allele is enough to give the trait. Written with a capital letter (A).
Dihybrid cross A cross tracing two genes in which both parents are heterozygous for both: AaBb × AaBb. (This course's definition.) It gives a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 phenotype ratio.
F1 cross A cross between F1 individuals (or an F1 self-fertilized), for example Aa × Aa. It produces the F2.
F1 generation The first filial generation: the offspring of the parental cross. When the parents are true-breeding for different traits, all F1 are heterozygous hybrids and show the dominant trait.
F2 cross A cross between F2 individuals (or an F2 self-fertilized). Mendel self-fertilized F2 plants to tell the true-breeding AA from the Aa.
F2 generation The second filial generation: the offspring of the F1 cross. The recessive trait reappears in the F2.
Gamete A haploid reproductive cell (egg, sperm, or the ovule's egg and the pollen's sperm in plants) carrying one allele of each gene.
Genotype The combination of alleles an individual has for a gene (or genes): AA, Aa or aa.
Heterozygous Having two different alleles of a gene: Aa.
Homozygous Having two identical alleles of a gene: AA or aa.
Hybridization Interbreeding between two different varieties (strains) or species. Mendel's crosses between true-breeding strains are hybridizations, and their offspring are hybrids.
Locus The place on a chromosome where a gene sits. The two alleles of a gene in a diploid cell are at the same locus on the two homologs.
Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment The segregation of one gene's alleles is independent of the segregation of another gene's alleles (for genes on different chromosomes), so all combinations of alleles appear in gametes in equal proportions.
Mendel's Law of Segregation The two alleles of a gene separate (segregate) equally into gametes, so half the gametes carry one allele and half carry the other.
Monohybrid cross A cross in which both parents are heterozygous for the one gene being traced: Aa × Aa. (This course's definition.)
Parental (P) generation The first generation in a series of crosses: here the true-breeding parents (written P or P₁).
Parental cross The cross between the two parents of the P generation, for example true-breeding yellow AA × true-breeding green aa. It produces the F1.
Phenotype The observable trait: yellow or green seeds. AA and Aa can have the same phenotype.
Punnett square A grid for predicting a cross: one parent's gametes and their frequencies go across the top, the other's down the side, and each box is a possible offspring genotype. Named after the British geneticist Reginald Punnett.
Recessive The trait (or allele) that does not show in the F1, and shows only in homozygotes (aa). Written with a lowercase letter (a).
Segregate To separate. The two alleles of a gene segregate into different gametes, because homologous chromosomes separate in anaphase I.
Testcross A cross of an individual with an unknown genotype to a homozygous recessive individual. The offspring's phenotypes reveal the unknown parent's gametes, and so its genotype.
True-breeding A strain whose offspring look the same as the parents, generation after generation, when bred among themselves: homozygous for the trait.
Zygote The fertilized egg, formed by the random union of two gametes, one from each parent. It has two alleles of each gene.

Notes

Everything you are expected to know for this module, in the order the learning objectives ask for it. Read it once, then use the checklist at the end.

IN THESE NOTES1 · Mendel's approach2 · Segregation and meiosis3 · Genotypes, gametes and offspring for one gene4 · Independent assortment and meiosis5 · Two genes: genotypes, gametes, offspring6 · Testcrosses and working backwards7 · Exam checklist
THE BIG IDEA

Each gene has two alleles that segregate equally into gametes, because homologs separate in anaphase I. Genes on different chromosomes assort independently, because pairs line up independently in metaphase I. With a Punnett square or the AND and OR rules, any cross can be predicted.

SECTION 1OBJECTIVE 1

Mendel's approach

  • He crossed garden peas (1856 to 1864), following seven contrasting traits.
  • True-breeding strains: offspring look like the parents generation after generation.
  • One trait at a time, with easily contrasted forms.
  • Counted the offspring, looking for ratios; others only noted presence or absence.
  • Hybridization = crossing different varieties. Mendel controlled crosses by removing anthers, dusting pollen and bagging flowers.
CROSSWHAT HAPPENSRESULT
Parental crossTrue-breeding AA × aaF1: all Aa, all dominant
F1 crossAa × Aa (or self)F2: 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa; 3 : 1
F2 crossF2 × F2 (or self)Tells AA (true-breeding) from Aa
Monohybrid crossBoth heterozygous for one gene (Aa × Aa)3 : 1
Dihybrid crossBoth heterozygous for two genes (AaBb × AaBb)9 : 3 : 3 : 1
TestcrossUnknown × homozygous recessiveReveals the unknown genotype
SECTION 2OBJECTIVE 4

Segregation and meiosis

  • The big picture: every Mendel problem is one movie: parents → gametes (one allele each) → fertilization → offspring. Segregation reflects homologs separating in anaphase I.
  • Law of Segregation: the two alleles of a gene separate equally into gametes; each gamete gets one.
  • It happens because the alleles are on homologous chromosomes, which separate in anaphase I.
  • An F1 Aa germ cell: after S, A A and a a; anaphase I sends A one way and a the other; after meiosis II, 2 A gametes and 2 a gametes.
SECTION 3OBJECTIVES 2 AND 3

Genotypes, gametes and offspring for one gene

  • Dominant = shows in the F1 of two true-breeding parents; recessive = hidden in the F1, back in a quarter of the F2.
  • Genotype (AA, Aa, aa) vs. phenotype (yellow, green). Homozygous AA or aa; heterozygous Aa; a heterozygote for a recessive condition is a carrier.
  • Gametes: AA → all A; aa → all a; Aa → 1/2 A, 1/2 a.
  • 1/2 vs. 1/4: an Aa parent's meiosis gives A, A, a, a, so p(A gamete) = 1/2. That is one gamete from one parent. An AA offspring needs an A egg AND an A sperm from two separate meioses: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. The A and a inside the Aa parent came from an earlier generation.
  • Both/and → multiply independent events (1/2 × 1/2). Either/or → add outcomes that can't happen together (1/4 + 1/2).
  • Aa × Aa → 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa, 1/4 aa; 3/4 dominant, 1/4 recessive. Among dominant offspring, 1/3 AA and 2/3 Aa.
  • A Punnett square is those probabilities as a grid: gametes outside, offspring inside.
Aa × AaGenotypes 1 : 2 : 1 · phenotypes 3 : 1
Aa × aaGenotypes 1 Aa : 1 aa · phenotypes 1 : 1
AA × aaAll Aa, all dominant
SECTION 4OBJECTIVE 5

Independent assortment and meiosis

  • Independent assortment reflects each pair of chromosomes lining up at random in metaphase I, so an AaBb plant makes AB, Ab, aB and ab gametes, 1/4 each.
  • Law of Independent Assortment: the alleles of one gene segregate independently of the alleles of another (genes on different chromosomes).
  • It happens because homologous pairs line up independently in metaphase I: AaBb → AB, Ab, aB, ab, 1/4 each.
  • One germ cell makes only 2 kinds of gamete (AB + ab, or Ab + aB); the whole organism makes all 4.
  • No independent assortment in mitosis. Genes close together on one chromosome are linked and do not assort independently (a later module).
  • Nondisjunction in meiosis I breaks segregation; nondisjunction in meiosis II doesn't break independent assortment (the combination was set in meiosis I).
SECTION 5OBJECTIVES 6, 7 AND 8

Two genes: genotypes, gametes, offspring

  • Write genotypes gene by gene: AaBb. A phenotype like "yellow round" covers several genotypes: A_ B_.
  • Parents → gametes: AAbb → Ab only; aaBB → aB only; AaBb → AB, Ab, aB, ab.
  • Probability first: solve each gene separately and multiply. p(AaBb) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4; p(yellow round) = 3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16.
  • Same answer as a picture: AaBb × AaBb is a 4 × 4 square, 16 boxes, 9 genotypes, 4 phenotypes: 9 A_B_ : 3 A_bb : 3 aaB_ : 1 aabb. Or two 2 × 2 squares, combined with AND.
  • Rows and columns = the number of gamete types of each parent.
  • Three or more genes: gamete types = 2ⁿ, n = number of heterozygous genes (BbLlRr → 8; BBLlRr → 4). For one offspring genotype, multiply gene by gene (AaBBCcDd × AaBbCcdd → aaBBccdd = 1/4 × 1/2 × 1/4 × 1/2 = 1/64).
SECTION 6OBJECTIVES 9 AND 10

Testcrosses and working backwards

  • Testcross: unknown (dominant phenotype) × homozygous recessive. All dominant offspring → homozygous; about half recessive → heterozygous.
  • Two genes: test with aabb and read each gene on its own. Brown long × bbll → all brown, half short → BB Ll.
  • Working backwards: 3 : 1 → both parents heterozygous; 1 : 1 → one heterozygous, one homozygous recessive; all dominant → at least one parent homozygous dominant; 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 → both parents dihybrid.
  • TtRr × ttrr → TtRr, Ttrr, ttRr, ttrr, 1/4 each; never TtRR.
SECTION 7

Exam checklist

You're ready when you can:

  • Explain how true-breeding strains, single traits and counting let Mendel find his laws.
  • Write the parents' genotypes, their gametes and the offspring from a written description of a cross.
  • Predict genotype and phenotype ratios for one-gene crosses with a Punnett square and with the AND/OR rules.
  • Show where segregation (anaphase I) and independent assortment (metaphase I) happen in meiosis.
  • Keep genotype and phenotype apart when tracing two genes.
  • Predict dihybrid crosses with a 16-box square or with two small squares and multiplication.
  • Design and interpret a testcross, for one gene or two.
  • Work out parents' genotypes from offspring ratios.
  • Count gamete types with 2ⁿ for any number of heterozygous genes.
COMMON MIX-UPGenotype ratio ≠ phenotype ratio (1 : 2 : 1 vs. 3 : 1). AND means multiply, OR means add. A testcross uses the homozygous recessive. And 2ⁿ counts only the heterozygous genes.

INFOGRAPHIC 1 · THE WHOLE MODULE ON ONE PAGE
MODULE 3.3 · PART 1

Mendel's experiments

Breeders had crossed plants for centuries without finding rules. What did Mendel do differently, and what did he see?

1How it all fits: what Mendel saw, why it happens, how to predict
There's a lot to keep track of in this module. It all hangs on one idea from the textbook: the laws of inheritance are what chromosomes do in meiosis. Mendel saw ratios; meiosis explains them; the tools predict them.1,2
1Why Mendel saw what others missed
Gregor Mendel, a monk in Brno, crossed garden peas (Pisum sativum) from 1856 to 1863. Plant breeders had done hybridization experiments before him, but none found rules. Mendel did, because of three choices.3,4
2P, F1, F2: one trait disappears and comes back
Mendel crossed true-breeding strains that differed in one trait. The result in the first generation was always the same: only one of the two traits showed.3,1
MODULE 3.3 · PART 2

One gene: the principle of segregation

Why does a trait that vanishes in the F1 come back in exactly a quarter of the F2?

1Segregation, tracked: one chromosome pair from P to F2
The textbook puts it in one line: "Segregation of alleles reflects the separation of chromosomes in meiosis." Watch one pair of chromosomes travel through two generations. Gold chromosomes came from the yellow-seed parent, green ones from the green-seed parent.1
1The principle of segregation
Mendel explained 3 : 1 with a few simple ideas, written here in today's words. The last one is the Law of Segregation, and meiosis is the reason it works.1,2
2From 1/2 to 1/4: why two A gametes don't mean AA is 1/2
The dividing cell shows 2 A and 2 a, which is 1/2. Yet AA is 1/4. Both are right, because they answer different questions: one is about a gamete from one parent, the other about an offspring from two parents.1,2
2Predicting crosses with probability: genotype and phenotype ratios
The law of segregation says what the gametes are, and that is all you need to predict a cross. Every probability is between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain), and two rules combine them.1,2
3The Punnett square: those probabilities in a grid
A Punnett square is a picture of the probabilities you just worked out: the same four outcomes, laid out as a grid. For the F1 cross Aa × Aa, a monohybrid cross (both parents heterozygous for the one gene traced), it gives Mendel's 3 : 1.1,2
MODULE 3.3 · PART 3

Two or more genes: independent assortment

When two traits are followed at once, does inheriting one affect inheriting the other?

1Two genes at once: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1
Next Mendel crossed strains differing in two traits: seed color (A yellow, a green) and seed shape (B round, b wrinkled).1,2
2Independent assortment, tracked: two chromosome pairs from P to F2
The textbook again: "Independent assortment reflects the random alignment of chromosomes in meiosis." Same movie as before, with two genes on two different chromosome pairs: seed color (A) on a long pair, seed shape (B) on a short pair.1
2Independent assortment comes from meiosis
The Law of Independent Assortment: the alleles of one gene segregate into gametes independently of the alleles of another. For genes on different chromosomes, the reason is metaphase I: each homologous pair lines up independently of the others.1,3
3Two genes with probability: both/and, gene by gene
Because the genes assort independently, a two-gene problem is just two one-gene problems. Take one question: brown long-tailed BbLl mice mate. What fraction of the offspring are also BbLl?1,3
4One big Punnett square: 16 boxes
You can also draw every combination. Each heterozygous parent makes four kinds of gametes, 1/4 each, so the square needs 4 rows and 4 columns: 16 equally likely boxes. It gives the same answer: AaBb is 4 of the 16 boxes, or 1/4.1
4Two small squares and the AND rule
The third way to the same answer: one 2 × 2 square for each gene, then multiply. Two small squares replace one 4 × 4.1,3
5The testcross
A yellow seed could be AA or Aa: same phenotype, different genotype. A testcross tells them apart by crossing the unknown with a homozygous recessive, which can only give a.4
5Testcrosses with two genes
The offspring of a cross tell you about the parents. A testcross with an aabb (here bbll) tester shows exactly which gametes the unknown parent made, one gene at a time.1,3
6Counting gametes and offspring for many genes
Independent assortment works for any number of genes on different chromosomes. Two counting tricks handle them.1,3

How Mendel set up his experiments

1 · TRUE-BREEDING STRAINSStart from strains that never changeEach strain Mendel used was true-breeding: bred among themselves, yellow-seeded plants gave only yellow seeds, generation after generation. Others used complex, poorly defined plants.
2 · ONE TRAIT AT A TIMEFollow one contrasting traitHe followed one trait (or a few) with easily contrasted forms, such as yellow vs. green seeds. Breeders who followed many traits at once saw inheritance so complicated that no pattern showed.

Part 2 · One gene: the principle of segregation

Segregation, tracked: one chromosome pair from P to F2
INFOGRAPHIC 5
INTERACTIVE · 6 STAGES · ONE GENE

From true-breeding parents to 3 : 1

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 6
P GENERATIONTwo true-breeding parentsA true-breeding yellow plant is AA: both chromosomes of the pair carry A. A true-breeding green plant is aa. Both are diploid: two of each chromosome.
MEIOSIS IN THE PARENTSOne chromosome per gameteMeiosis puts one chromosome of each pair into each gamete. An AA plant has only A to give, so every gamete is A; every aa gamete is a.
FERTILIZATION · F1One from each parentAn A gamete meets an a gamete: every F1 plant is Aa, with one gold and one green chromosome. All are yellow because A is dominant, but the a allele is still there, hidden.
ANAPHASE I IN THE F1This is segregationIn an F1 germ cell, the homologs separate in anaphase I: the A chromosome goes one way, the a chromosome the other. That physical separation is Mendel's law of segregation.
THE F1'S GAMETESHalf A, half aAfter meiosis II, half the F1's gametes carry A and half carry a. That 1 : 1 is the whole secret of the 3 : 1.
F2Random union gives 1 : 2 : 1Any egg can meet any sperm: AA, Aa, aA, aa, equally likely. Genotypes 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa; phenotypes 3 yellow : 1 green. The green trait "skipped" the F1 and came back, because the F1 carried it hidden.
The principle of segregation
INFOGRAPHIC 6
INTERACTIVE · MEIOSIS IN AN F1 PLANT

Where segregation happens

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 4
THE GERM CELLOne A, one aAn F1 plant's germ cell has the A allele on one homolog and the a allele on the other.
AFTER S PHASEBoth alleles copiedEach chromosome is now two sister chromatids: A A on one homolog, a a on the other.
ANAPHASE ISegregation, physicallyThe homologous chromosomes separate in anaphase I, so the A copies go to one pole and the a copies to the other. This separation is the segregation Mendel inferred from his ratios.
THE GAMETESHalf A, half aAfter meiosis II, two gametes carry A and two carry a: 1/2 A, 1/2 a, exactly as the law predicts.
From 1/2 to 1/4: why two A gametes don't mean AA is 1/2
INFOGRAPHIC 7
WALK THROUGH IT · 5 STEPS · THREE GENERATIONS

From one cell's gametes to one offspring

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 5
LOOK BACK A GENERATIONThe A and a came from this plant's own parentsThe cell in the slides is already Aa because of an earlier fertilization: one AA parent, one aa parent. That mother and father are finished. They are not the two sets in the calculation.
ONE PARENT · ONE MEIOSISp(A gamete) = 1/2This one plant's cell copies its DNA, then divides twice, ending in A, A, a, a. 2 of 4 gametes carry A. That 1/2 is about one gamete.
THE SECOND SETNow two Aa plants mateA new plant takes one gamete from its mother and one from its father. So there are two separate meioses, one in each F1 parent, each giving 1/2 A and 1/2 a. This is the other set you need to consider.
BOTH MUST HAPPENp(AA) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4AA needs an A egg and an A sperm. Getting an A from one parent doesn't guarantee an A from the other, so you multiply.
SEE IT AS FRACTIONSHalf of a halfHalf of all offspring got an A egg. Only half of those also got an A sperm. That leaves a quarter of all the offspring: AA.
Predicting crosses with probability: genotype and phenotype ratios
INFOGRAPHIC 8
INTERACTIVE · Aa × Aa

From gametes to ratios

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 5
THE GAMETESHalf A, half aAn Aa parent gives A 1/2 and a 1/2, because the alleles segregate.
BOTH/AND = MULTIPLYOne egg AND one spermEach offspring needs an egg and a sperm. They are independent events, so multiply: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
EITHER/OR = ADDTwo ways to be AaA from mom and a from dad, or a from mom and A from dad. They can't both happen, so add: 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2.
GENOTYPE RATIO1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aaA genotype ratio counts allele combinations: 1/4 AA, 1/2 Aa, 1/4 aa.
PHENOTYPE RATIO3 dominant : 1 recessiveA phenotype ratio counts what you see. A is dominant, so AA and Aa are both yellow: 1/4 + 1/2 = 3/4. Only aa shows the recessive green: 1/4.
INFOGRAPHIC 9
INTERACTIVE · THE TEXTBOOK'S POD OF FOUR PEAS

The same two rules, used together

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 3
EITHER/OR = ADDOutcomes that can't happen togetherOne seed can't be both AA and Aa, so the chance it is AA or Aa is 1/4 + 1/2 = 3/4.
BOTH/AND = MULTIPLYIndependent events togetherEach seed comes from a separate fertilization, so they are independent. The chance the seed by the stem is green and the other three yellow: 1/4 × 3/4 × 3/4 × 3/4 = 27/256.
USE BOTHExactly one green, any positionThe green seed can be in any of 4 positions (OR), each with probability 27/256 (AND): 4 × 27/256 = 108/256, about 42%.

Build the square

Tap the buttons, or Next, to click through all 5
THE OUTSIDEThe gametesLetters on the outside are one parent's gametes across the top and the other parent's down the side, each with its probability: an Aa parent gives A 1/2 and a 1/2.
THE INSIDEThe offspringEach box inside is a zygote: the gamete in its row joined with the gamete in its column. Its probability is the row's × the column's: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

Why Mendel saw what others missed

Gregor Mendel, a monk in Brno, crossed garden peas (Pisum sativum) from 1856 to 1863. Plant breeders had done hybridization experiments before him, but none found rules. Mendel did, because of three choices.3,4

3 · COUNT THE OFFSPRINGLook for numbersHe counted every offspring and looked for statistical patterns. Others only noted whether a trait was present or absent. Counting is what revealed 3 : 1 and 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

07 / 27 · PART 1 · LOCK IT IN

Lock it in · Part 1

  1. Mendel succeeded because he used true-breeding strains, followed one trait at a time, and counted the offspring.
  2. Parental cross (true-breeding AA × aa) → F1, all Aa, all showing the dominant trait.
  3. F1 cross (Aa × Aa) → F2, with the recessive trait back in a 3 : 1 ratio: it "skips a generation".
  4. The trait that shows in the F1 of two true-breeding parents is the dominant one.

15 / 27 · PART 2 · LOCK IT IN

Lock it in · Part 2

  1. Segregation: the two alleles of a gene separate equally into gametes (1/2 A, 1/2 a). It happens in anaphase I, when homologs separate.
  2. 1/2 is about one gamete from one parent. 1/4 is about one offspring from two parents: an A egg (1/2) AND an A sperm (1/2).
  3. Gametes first: Aa gives 1/2 A, 1/2 a. Both/and → multiply (independent events). Either/or → add (outcomes that can't happen together).
  4. Aa × Aa (a monohybrid cross): genotypes 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa; phenotypes 3 dominant : 1 recessive.
  5. A Punnett square is the same probabilities as a grid: gametes outside, offspring inside.

Independent assortment comes from meiosis

The Law of Independent Assortment: the alleles of one gene segregate into gametes independently of the alleles of another. For genes on different chromosomes, the reason is metaphase I: each homologous pair lines up independently of the others.1,3

Tap a button to explore
WAY 1 · HALF OF ALL GERM CELLSAB and abA and B face the same pole: this cell's gametes are AB and ab.
WAY 2 · THE OTHER HALFAb and aBThe short pair is flipped: this cell's gametes are Ab and aB.
ACROSS MANY GERM CELLS1/4 eachBoth ways are equally likely, so over many cells: AB, Ab, aB, ab, 1/4 each. With the AND rule: p(AB) = p(A) × p(B) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.
TAP ONEWhich way will the pairs face?Pink came from the mother, blue from the father. Each pair's orientation is random.

A yellow seed could be AA or Aa: same phenotype, different genotype. A testcross tells them apart by crossing the unknown with a homozygous recessive, which can only give a.4

Lock it in · Part 3

  1. Dihybrid cross (AaBb × AaBb) → phenotypes 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 (9 A_B_ : 3 A_bb : 3 aaB_ : 1 aabb); 9 genotypes.
  2. Independent assortment: each gene's alleles segregate independently of another's (genes on different chromosomes), because homologous pairs line up independently in metaphase I. AaBb → AB, Ab, aB, ab, 1/4 each.
  3. One germ cell makes 2 kinds of gamete; the whole organism makes all 4.
  4. Three ways to the same answer: probability gene by gene, one big square (rows × columns = gamete types of each parent), or two small squares combined with AND.
  5. A testcross (unknown × homozygous recessive) reveals the unknown genotype: all dominant → homozygous; half recessive → heterozygous. With two genes, read one gene at a time.
  6. Gamete types = 2ⁿ, n = number of heterozygous genes.

Quiz

36 questions on Mendel’s experiments, segregation, Punnett squares, probability, testcrosses and independent assortment, including the class questions. Pick an answer to see whether it is right and why.

QUESTION 1 OF 36Which was NOT one of the reasons Mendel discovered rules that other breeders missed?

Correct. Not quite. Following many traits at once gave inheritance too complicated to see a pattern.

QUESTION 2 OF 36A true-breeding strain is one that:

Correct. Not quite. True-breeding strains are homozygous for the trait.

QUESTION 3 OF 36True-breeding plants with yellow seeds are crossed with true-breeding plants with green seeds. All F1 plants have yellow seeds. Which trait is caused by the dominant allele (A)?

Correct. Not quite. The trait that shows in the F1 of two true-breeding parents is dominant.

QUESTION 4 OF 36The F1 of that cross are allowed to self-fertilize. What fraction of the F2 are both yellow AND heterozygous?

Correct. Not quite. Aa is 2 of the 4 boxes of the Punnett square, and every Aa seed is yellow.

QUESTION 5 OF 36Why does a recessive trait seem to "skip a generation"?

Correct. Not quite. A quarter of the F2 are homozygous recessive.

QUESTION 6 OF 36Mendel's F2 ratio across all seven traits was:

Correct. Not quite. 14,949 dominant : 5,010 recessive.

QUESTION 7 OF 36The principle of segregation says that:

Correct. Not quite. Half the gametes of an Aa carry A and half carry a.

QUESTION 8 OF 36Where in meiosis does segregation occur?

Correct. Not quite. The A and a alleles are on homologous chromosomes.

QUESTION 9 OF 36An F1 plant is Aa. What proportion of its gametes carry A?

Correct. Not quite. Segregation: 1/2 A, 1/2 a.

QUESTION 10 OF 36In a Punnett square, the letters on the outside represent:

Correct. Not quite. The inside boxes are the offspring genotypes.

QUESTION 11 OF 36Aa × Aa gives which genotype ratio?

Correct. Not quite. 3 : 1 is the phenotype ratio.

QUESTION 12 OF 36Which rule do you use for the chance of AA OR Aa?

Correct. Not quite. 1/4 + 1/2 = 3/4: mutually exclusive outcomes are added.

QUESTION 13 OF 36Which rule do you use for the chance of getting A from mom AND a from dad?

Correct. Not quite. Independent events: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

QUESTION 14 OF 36Xeroderma pigmentosum is a recessive skin condition. A woman homozygous for the dominant allele and a homozygous man with the condition have a child. What is the probability the child has the condition?

Correct. Not quite. Every child gets the dominant allele from the mother and is a heterozygous carrier.

QUESTION 15 OF 36Among the yellow seeds of an Aa × Aa cross, what fraction are AA?

Correct. Not quite. Yellow is 3 boxes: 1 AA and 2 Aa.

QUESTION 16 OF 36A testcross crosses an unknown individual with:

Correct. Not quite. The recessive tester only gives recessive alleles, so the offspring reveal the unknown's gametes.

QUESTION 17 OF 36An unknown yellow plant × a green (aa) plant gives half yellow and half green offspring. The unknown is:

Correct. Not quite. An AA parent would give all yellow offspring.

QUESTION 18 OF 36A heterozygous person who has one copy of a recessive allele but not the recessive trait is a:

Correct. Not quite. Two carriers have a 1/4 chance of an affected child.

QUESTION 19 OF 36An Aa parent's meiosis gives A, A, a, a gametes. Why is p(AA) in Aa × Aa 1/4 and not 1/2?

Correct. Not quite. p(A gamete) = 1/2 for each parent. Both must happen, so multiply: 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

QUESTION 20 OF 36What cross gives a 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 phenotypic ratio?

Correct. Not quite. A dihybrid cross, with genes that assort independently.

QUESTION 21 OF 36True-breeding yellow wrinkled (AAbb) × true-breeding green round (aaBB). The F1 are:

Correct. Not quite. Yellow and round are both dominant.

QUESTION 22 OF 36Where in meiosis does independent assortment occur?

Correct. Not quite. Each pair's orientation is random relative to the others.

QUESTION 23 OF 36A germ cell (2n = 4) is heterozygous for two genes on different chromosomes. How many kinds of gametes can that ONE germ cell make?

Correct. Not quite. It lines up only one way. The whole organism makes 4 kinds.

QUESTION 24 OF 36A cell in anaphase I has A pulling away from a and B pulling away from b. What principle does it illustrate?

Correct. Not quite. One cell shows only one orientation, so it can't show independent assortment by itself.

QUESTION 25 OF 36Two cells line their pairs up in the two different possible ways, and in each the homologs separate. What do they illustrate?

Correct. Not quite. Different orientations show independent assortment; homologs separating shows segregation.

QUESTION 26 OF 36If nondisjunction of the blue (A/a) chromosome pair occurs in meiosis I, which law is violated?

Correct. Not quite. A and a go into the same gamete instead of separating.

QUESTION 27 OF 36For a TtRr individual, how many unique gamete types exist? For a ttrr individual?

Correct. Not quite. TR, Tr, tR, tr vs. only tr.

QUESTION 28 OF 36Which genotype would you NOT expect among the offspring of TtRr × ttrr?

Correct. Not quite. The ttrr parent only gives r, so no offspring can be RR.

QUESTION 29 OF 36How many rows and columns does the Punnett square for AaBb × AaBb need?

Correct. Not quite. Each parent makes 4 kinds of gamete.

QUESTION 30 OF 36True-breeding brown long-tailed mice × true-breeding yellow short-tailed mice give all brown long-tailed F1. Two F1 mate. What fraction of their offspring have the F1 genotype?

Correct. Not quite. p(Bb) × p(Ll) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4 = 4/16.

QUESTION 31 OF 36You capture a mouse with brown fur and a long tail but don't know its genotype. What cross will definitively tell you its genotype?

Correct. Not quite. A testcross.

QUESTION 32 OF 36You cross the captured mouse with a mouse true-breeding for yellow fur and a short tail. All offspring have brown fur; half have long tails, half short. The captured mouse was:

Correct. Not quite. No yellow offspring → BB; half short → Ll.

QUESTION 33 OF 36How many distinct gamete genotypes can a BbLlRr mouse make?

Correct. Not quite. 2³ = 8.

QUESTION 34 OF 36How many distinct gamete genotypes can a BBLlRr mouse make?

Correct. Not quite. Only the heterozygous genes count: 2² = 4 (BLR, BLr, BlR, Blr).

QUESTION 35 OF 36Four genes on different chromosomes: AaBBCcDd × AaBbCcdd. Expected frequency of aaBBccdd?

Correct. Not quite. aa 1/4, BB 1/2, cc 1/4, dd 1/2.

QUESTION 36 OF 36Do chromosomes 4 and 5 of a pea plant assort independently during mitosis?

Correct. Not quite. Independent assortment happens only in meiosis I; in mitosis every daughter gets every chromosome.

Guiding questions · Crosses, Punnett squares and probability

These are the questions this module is built to answer. Try each one from memory, then tap it to check.

Q1  What happens during a parental cross, an F1 cross, a monohybrid cross, and a dihybrid cross?

Parental cross: two true-breeding parents with different traits are crossed (AA × aa); all offspring, the F1, are heterozygous (Aa) and show the dominant trait.

F1 cross: two F1 individuals are crossed (or an F1 self-fertilizes), Aa × Aa, producing the F2, where the recessive trait reappears (3 : 1).

Monohybrid cross: both parents are heterozygous for the one gene traced (Aa × Aa): genotypes 1 : 2 : 1, phenotypes 3 : 1.

Dihybrid cross: both parents are heterozygous for two genes (AaBb × AaBb): phenotypes 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.

Q2  What do the letters on the outside and the inside of a Punnett square represent?

Outside: the alleles carried by each parent's gametes, one parent across the top and the other down the side, with their frequencies (Aa → A 1/2, a 1/2).

Inside: the offspring genotypes (zygotes), each formed by the gamete in that row joining the gamete in that column; each box's probability is the row's times the column's.

Q3  Given the parental and F1 crosses shown at the start of the lecture, why do we often say that recessive traits “skip a generation”?

In the parental cross (AA × aa) every F1 offspring is Aa and shows the dominant trait, so the recessive trait disappears in the F1. But the F1 still carry the recessive allele, so in the F1 cross (Aa × Aa) a quarter of the F2 are aa and show it again: it seems to "skip" the F1 generation.

Q4  What is the difference between a genotype ratio and a phenotype ratio?

A genotype ratio compares allele combinations (Aa × Aa: 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa). A phenotype ratio compares observable traits (3 yellow : 1 green). With dominance, AA and Aa look the same, so the two ratios differ.

Q5  Where in meiosis does segregation occur? How does the law of segregation help us make predictions about the alleles that are found in gametes?

In anaphase I of meiosis, when the homologous chromosomes carrying the two alleles separate to opposite poles.

It tells us each gamete gets exactly one allele of each gene, and that a heterozygote's two alleles go into gametes equally: AA → all A; aa → all a; Aa → 1/2 A and 1/2 a. Those gamete frequencies go on the outside of a Punnett square.

Q6  How do the ‘both/and’ and ‘either/or’ rules work?

Both/and (multiplication rule): the probability that two independent events both happen is the product of their probabilities. p(A from mom AND a from dad) = 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4.

Either/or (addition rule): the probability that one or another of mutually exclusive outcomes happens is the sum. p(AA OR Aa) = 1/4 + 1/2 = 3/4.

Guiding questions · Independent assortment and two or more genes

These are the questions this module is built to answer. Try each one from memory, then tap it to check.

Q7  Where in meiosis does independent assortment occur? How does the law of independent assortment help us make predictions about the alleles that are found in gametes?

In metaphase I (with the separation in anaphase I): each homologous pair lines up independently of every other pair, so which allele of one gene goes to a pole doesn't affect which allele of another gene goes with it.

So for genes on different chromosomes, every combination of alleles is equally likely in gametes: AaBb → AB, Ab, aB, ab, 1/4 each (1/2 × 1/2).

Q8  What cross gives you a 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio?

A dihybrid cross: AaBb × AaBb, where the two genes assort independently and each has a dominant and a recessive allele affecting a different trait. 9 A_B_ : 3 A_bb : 3 aaB_ : 1 aabb.

Q9  Assume we are tracing the inheritance of two genes each located on separate chromosomes in an organism with 2n = 4. How many different kinds of gametes can one germ cell, heterozygous for both genes, make? How many different kinds of gametes can that whole organism make (when considering the whole population of germ cells)?

One germ cell: 2 kinds of gamete. It lines up one way in metaphase I, giving either AB and ab, or Ab and aB.

The whole organism: 4 kinds (AB, Ab, aB, ab), because half its germ cells line up one way and half the other.

Q10  Why is nondisjunction during meiosis II not a violation of independent assortment?

Independent assortment happens in meiosis I, when homologous pairs line up independently and separate. By meiosis II, the combination of chromosomes in each cell is already set. Nondisjunction in meiosis II only fails to separate sister chromatids, copies of the same allele, so it changes the number of copies in a gamete, not which alleles of different genes go together.

Q11  How many rows and columns do you need in a Punnett square? When might you use two Punnett Squares together instead of one big Punnett square? Explain your answers.

One row for each kind of gamete one parent can make and one column for each kind the other can make (Aa × Aa: 2 × 2; AaBb × AaBb: 4 × 4; AaBb × aabb: 4 × 1).

Use two (or more) small squares, one per gene, when the genes assort independently: solve each gene separately and multiply the probabilities (AND rule). It is faster and less error-prone than a 16- or 64-box square, especially when you need one specific genotype or phenotype.

Q12  How can you determine which trait is dominant, when two true-breeding parents are crossed? Consider a situation where we are tracing inheritance of one gene and the situation where we are tracing inheritance of two genes.

One gene: the trait that appears in the F1 of two true-breeding parents is dominant; the one that disappears is recessive (yellow × green → all yellow, so yellow is dominant).

Two genes: look at each trait separately in the F1. Yellow wrinkled × green round → all yellow round, so yellow is dominant to green and round is dominant to wrinkled.

Q13  What is a test cross and what does it allow you to figure out?

A testcross crosses an individual of unknown genotype (with the dominant phenotype) to a homozygous recessive individual. Because the tester only gives recessive alleles, the offspring's phenotypes show which alleles the unknown parent's gametes carried.

It tells you the unknown genotype: all offspring dominant → homozygous (AA); about half recessive → heterozygous (Aa). With two genes, read each gene separately (all brown, half short-tailed → BB Ll).

Q14  How can you figure out the number of unique gamete genotypes for an organism that is heterozygous for 3 or more genes? What about if an organism has a genotype with a mixture of heterozygous and homozygous genes?

Use 2ⁿ, where n is the number of genes for which the organism is heterozygous (assuming the genes assort independently): AaBbCc → 2³ = 8 kinds of gamete.

Homozygous genes give only one allele, so they don't add variety: BBLlRr → n = 2, 2² = 4 kinds (BLR, BLr, BlR, Blr). A branching diagram lists them all.
